newsitem.title: USA: NC jury considers fate of killer in race slayings.
newsitem.headline: NC jury considers fate of killer in race slayings.

text.p: Two alternate jurors released Wednesday from the sentencing phase of the trial of a white former paratrooper convicted of murdering two black people said they doubted the killer would get a death sentence.

Four alternates were dismissed before the jury began deliberations on whether James Burmeister, found guilty last Thursday in the racially motivated slayings of Michael James, 36, and Jackie Burden, 27, on Dec. 7 1995, should get the death penalty.
Alternate juror Gary Leviner, a 51-year-old pastor, said Burmeister's youth and lack of life experience would have made it difficult to sentence him to die, despite the brutality of his crime.
"He was a good young man before he came to Fort Bragg," Leviner said. "He was away from home for the first time and got mixed up with the wrong people."
Another alternate juror, who asked not to be identified, said he believed the jury made the right decision in finding Burmeister guilty but expressed doubt that he would be sentenced to death.

The jury found Burmeister, 21, shot the couple at close range in December 1995 as they walked in Fayetteville, which adjoins Fort Bragg, home to the U.S. Army's elite 82nd Airborne Division. Burmeister was drinking in a bar with fellow soldiers Randy Meadows and Malcolm Wright on the base before the murders.

Meadows pleaded guilty to involvement in the crime and became the prosecution's key witness. He testified that he never believed Burmeister would shoot anyone, even after Burmeister left the car with a pistol in his belt.

Prosecutors said during the trial that Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web" tattoo, a skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a gay or black person. White supremacist and bomb-making literature and a Nazi flag were found at Burmeister's trailer.
